claims.statement: A baby 3 months old or younger with a rectal temperature of 100.4F (38C) or higher needs a pediatrician immediately, even if the baby appears well.
Fever in a young infant can be the only sign of a serious infection, because their immune systems are immature.
Rectal thermometers are the most accurate way to take a young infant's temperature.
For babies 3 to 6 months, call the doctor for fevers up to 102F (38.9C), or at any temperature if the baby seems unusually irritable, lethargic, or unwell.
For babies over 6 months, call the doctor for fevers above 102F lasting more than a day, or sooner if other concerning symptoms appear.
How a baby acts matters as much as the number: a feverish baby who drinks, cries normally, and responds to comfort is differently concerning than one who is limp, unresponsive, or cannot be consoled.
Babies should be placed on their backs for every sleep, naps included, until 1 year of age. Side sleeping is not safe.
Babies should sleep in the parents' room but on a separate firm flat surface (crib, bassinet, or play yard), ideally for at least the first 6 months.
Room sharing without bed sharing can reduce SIDS risk by as much as half.
The sleep space should be empty of pillows, blankets, bumpers, soft bedding, and toys; babies should never sleep on couches or armchairs.
By 2 months, most babies begin to smile at people, briefly calm themselves (hands to mouth), coo and make gurgling sounds, and try to look at a parent.
By 4 months, most babies smile spontaneously to get attention, chuckle, hold their head steady without support, push up on elbows, and take turns making sounds.
By 6 months, most babies know familiar people, roll from tummy to back, sit with support, and make squealing sounds.
Milestones describe what most children do by a given age (75% after the 2022 revision); a child not showing one is a reason to ask the pediatrician, not a verdict.
If a child loses skills they previously had at any age, that is a specific sign to talk to a doctor promptly.
Babies under about 6 months need only breast milk or properly prepared infant formula; no other food or drink is needed.
Do not give honey to babies under 12 months, not even tiny amounts — honey can carry botulism spores that cause infant botulism.
Solid foods are typically introduced around 6 months, when a baby can hold their head steady and shows interest in food; every baby's pace differs.
New foods can be introduced one at a time over a few days, which makes it easier to notice any reaction.
Keep small objects, hard round foods, and pieces smaller than a choke-test cylinder away from babies and toddlers; choking hazard is real before age 4.
All infants ride rear-facing starting with the first ride home from the hospital, and stay rear-facing as long as possible, up to the seat's height and weight limits.
Constant, undistracted supervision around water is the rule — most drownings of children 4 and younger happen during non-swim times, when nobody expected the child to be in water.
If an infant chokes and cannot breathe or cry, act immediately: back blows and chest thrusts for infants under 1, and learn them from a certified class before you need them.
By 2 months most babies try to look at their parents, briefly calm themselves, and take turns making sounds — early interaction is developmental work, not indulgence.
Taking turns with sounds and responding to a baby's bids for attention is listed developmental behavior at 2, 4, and 6 months — the back-and-forth itself is the curriculum.
Babies know familiar people by 6 months; consistent presence is how familiarity is built.
